# Map layers

Map layer (i) notes. Every layer covers the waterway's box, clipped to the currents model's water, so all layers share one coastline. Times are stored in UTC and labeled in New York time. All data are provisional and may be revised.

## Comfort

(method-comfort)=
### Comfort for small craft

Method
: The worst factor below for your boat, from HRRR wind, NWPS waves, the wave-current level and (kayaks) NECOFS current; for kayaks, the paddlers' 120 rule (air and water temperature together under 120 °F, when a dry suit is called for) raises a level. Water temperature does not count for the other boats. Steps follow Beaufort, WMO sea states and the NWS small craft advisory; the 30% rule, post-Fastnet (1979) capsize tests.

Caveats
: An indicative index derived from forecasts, not a determination of whether to go. Excludes gusts, visibility and thunderstorms. More than 24 hours back it rests on wind alone. The thresholds are judgments for typical boats of each length, not a standard; the code is open source (github.com/lhzn-io/lhzn-blue), so anyone can set their own and build an index on the same method.

[How the index is computed, with a worked example](https://longhorizon.blue/about/comfort-index/)

(method-map-comfort)=
### Comfort index (map)

Method
: The comfort index of a click's readout, for every NWPS wave cell (1.8 km) at the time bar's hour: HRRR wind from the nearest HRRR cell, NWPS waves, the wind-against-tide level and, for kayaks, the NECOFS current, by the steps for the boat set in the byline; for kayaks, air and water together under 120 °F (HRRR's air at the nearest forecast station) raise a level. Shore cells (harbors, coves) carry wind only. Shown as a score from 0 to 7: each factor runs linearly between its steps, so 1 is the Moderate step, 2 Uncomfortable and 3 Discomfort; past Discomfort it gains a point for each half of that step again (for a center console, 30, 40 and 50 kt of wind, or 1.5, 2 and 2.5 m of waves), and the worst factor sets the score. The shading runs from clear at 0 through pale pink to rose at 3, then raspberry and plum toward 7 (on the dark map, from dim plum to pale pink). NWS advisories keep their brick outline, apart from this scale. The Discomfort zones overlay marks where the score reaches 3, crosshatched within a fine outline, over this field or over wind, waves or currents.

Caveats
: The score places a cell between fixed thresholds; it is not a probability, and its fractions are as much a judgment as the steps. The shading excludes NWS advisories, which the masthead and the zone lines show and a click's readout includes. No shading beyond HRRR's 48-hour forecast. The map reaches 14 days back once the HRRR history loads (on the first step back past 24 hours); the wave, wind-against-tide and current models keep 24 hours back, so before that the score rests on HRRR wind alone and the key says so. Excludes gusts and tide rips.

(method-map-wat)=
### Wind against tide

Shows
: Where the tidal current runs against the waves and steepens them, on the wave model's 1.8 km cells, every 2 hours from 24 hours back to 72 hours ahead, in four levels: the current steepening the waves; steep, short seas likely; breaking seas likely; and the waves blocked by the current (they break at its edge). Arrows show where the opposing current runs. Clicking a cell gives the current, the waves and how much steeper they get. It is an overlay: the layer menu lays it over the wind, waves or currents layer (their arrows then stand for the overlay's), or shows it on its own.

Method
: The waves (height, peak period and direction) are the NWS NWPS forecast (SWAN {ref}`[1] <ref-booij1999swan>`); the current is the NECOFS FVCOM surface layer {ref}`[2] <ref-chen2006fvcom>` averaged over each wave cell. With r the current along the waves' direction divided by their deep-water speed (gT/2π), conservation of wave action gives how much closer together (wavelength) and higher the crests get while the period holds {ref}`[3] <ref-longuet1961currents>`; the waves stop where r reaches -0.25. Levels: steepening when the current makes the waves 20 percent steeper or more; steep at 60 percent, or at 20 percent when the waves reach a steepness of 1/25; breaking at r of -0.20, or at 60 percent with a steepness of 1/15; blocked at -0.25. Each level is what the current adds: wind waves in the Sound are often steep in slack water. Breaking and blocked need waves of 0.4 m (1.3 ft) or more. Nothing is shown where the current is under 0.3 m/s (0.6 kt) or the waves under 0.2 m. Drawn as tide-rip hatching, after the chart symbol for rips and overfalls {ref}`[4] <ref-noaa2019chart1>`: finer rows for the lower levels, the densest and heaviest kept for blocking. The patterns are fixed and do not rescale with the hours shown.

Caveats
: A model-derived index: not an observation and not an NWS product; NWS advisories take precedence. Linear, deep-water theory for waves entering the current from slack water. Excludes shoals, rips and overfalls finer than the cells (the Race, Plum Gut and Hell Gate in detail), boat wakes and wave groups. The thresholds are provisional and have not been validated against wave observations.

References: [1] {ref}`Booij, Ris and Holthuijsen (1999), the SWAN wave model <ref-booij1999swan>`; [2] {ref}`Chen, Beardsley and Cowles (2006), the FVCOM system <ref-chen2006fvcom>`; [3] {ref}`Longuet-Higgins and Stewart (1961), short gravity waves on steady non-uniform currents <ref-longuet1961currents>`; [4] {ref}`NOAA and NGA (2019), U.S. Chart No. 1 <ref-noaa2019chart1>`.

## Wind, waves and currents

(method-map-wind)=
### Wind (HRRR)

Shows
: Forecast wind 10 m above the surface on the model's own 3 km cells, shaded by speed, with arrows in the direction the wind blows toward; 14 days back to 48 hours ahead. The hours before the last 24 are a separate file, loaded when the time bar first goes back past them.

Method
: NOAA's High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) {ref}`[1] <ref-dowell2022hrrr>`, read through forcingkit. Each hour comes from the newest run that covers it: hourly runs reach 18 hours ahead, the 00, 06, 12 and 18 UTC runs 48 hours; a past hour comes from the run issued 1 hour before it (2 or 3 hours where that run is missing), and is kept for 14 days. Values are raw: no smoothing between cells. Cells HRRR counts as land are drawn fainter inland; land cells touching water (harbors, coves, the shore) are drawn like water, and a click there says it is a land cell.

Caveats
: A model forecast, not a measurement; the past hours are short-lead forecasts, not observations. Speeds follow the Units switch.

References: [1] {ref}`Dowell et al. (2022), the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) <ref-dowell2022hrrr>`.

(method-map-waves)=
### Waves (NWS model)

Shows
: Forecast significant wave height on the model's own 1.8 km cells, shaded by height, with arrows in the direction the waves travel; 24 hours back to 72 hours ahead.

Method
: The NWS Nearshore Wave Prediction System, which runs the SWAN spectral wave model {ref}`[1] <ref-booij1999swan>`, from the New York forecast office at 00 and 12 UTC on its CG1 grid, forced by the office's forecast winds. Each hour comes from the newest run that covers it. Colors: an ordered ramp after cmocean {ref}`[2] <ref-thyng2016cmocean>`.

Caveats
: A model forecast, not a measurement. The runs exclude currents; steepening where the tide opposes the waves is not represented.

References: [1] {ref}`Booij, Ris and Holthuijsen (1999), the SWAN wave model <ref-booij1999swan>`; [2] {ref}`Thyng et al. (2016), cmocean: colormaps for oceanography <ref-thyng2016cmocean>`.

(method-map-currents)=
### Surface currents

Shows
: Modeled currents in the top layer, on the model's own triangles, shaded by speed, with arrows in the direction of flow; 24 hours back to 72 hours ahead.

Method
: The NECOFS FVCOM forecast (NECOFS/UMASSD), every 2 hours {ref}`[1] <ref-chen2003fvcom>` {ref}`[2] <ref-chen2006fvcom>`. Colors follow one fixed scale on a logarithmic speed axis, from 0.02 to 3.1 m/s, with knots from 2026 NOAA CO-OPS current predictions (0.494 m/s, the median daily maximum across Long Island and Block Island Sound; 2.418 and 3.097 m/s, the median and annual daily maxima at Little Gull Island in the Race). The scale runs from near white through sage and teal to navy, after cmocean's tempo {ref}`[3] <ref-thyng2016cmocean>`, so faster water is darker. The dark theme reverses it on the same speeds, navy to near white, so faster water is lighter there. The same scale colors the currents in the 3D view, the Northeast Shelf maps and the lab's other viewers.

Caveats
: A model forecast, not a measurement. Speeds follow the Units switch.

[The same model in 3D, below the surface](https://longhorizon.blue/long-island-sound/currents-3d/)

References: [1] {ref}`Chen, Liu and Beardsley (2003), FVCOM <ref-chen2003fvcom>`; [2] {ref}`Chen, Beardsley and Cowles (2006), the FVCOM system <ref-chen2006fvcom>`; [3] {ref}`Thyng et al. (2016), cmocean: colormaps for oceanography <ref-thyng2016cmocean>`.

(method-map-radar)=
### Surface currents (HF radar)

Shows
: Measured surface currents, hourly, on 1 km cells, shaded by speed, with arrows in the direction of flow; the last 72 hours the network has published. Gold, from 0 to 0.5 m/s and the darkest gold above, is the site's color for measured currents; the model's currents run from sage through teal to navy, so the two layers are never confused.

Method
: Shore-based high-frequency radar measures the speed of the surface water toward or away from each site (a radial). Where two sites see the same cell at a good angle, the NOAA IOOS HF Radar National Network (HFRNet) combines their radials into an hourly total vector on a 1 km grid; NOAA NDBC serves the totals. In the western Sound the sites are the University of Connecticut's (LISICOS). The network keeps cells whose geometric dilution of precision is at most 1.25. Cells are drawn at the grid's own resolution; an hour with no total in a cell leaves it empty.

Caveats
: The top meter or so of the water, averaged over the hour and the cell. Coverage stops east of about Norwalk, and thins at the edges and near the shore. A click's readout flags a cell at the edge of that hour's coverage (a side neighbor without a total) and a total with weak geometry (GDOP above 1.0), where the speed and direction are less certain. Across the Sound the sites face each other, so the along-Sound part of the flow is the least constrained: against NOAA's current survey meters the tidal current has read weak at some cells and strong at others, and turned toward north-south at some, varying with season. The network publishes a few hours behind real time.

(method-current-phase)=
### Current at a reference point

Shows
: In the Tides view, under the time bar, the tidal current at one of four points along the Sound: the Race, the central Sound (Branford Reef, 5 miles south), Execution Rocks and Throgs Neck; or at NOAA's current meter at Groton, in the Thames River. Above the line is flood, below it ebb. The filled band is the NECOFS model's surface current (the light band); the fine line is NOAA's tidal current prediction; the vertical line is the time bar's hour. The label reads the phase there and the next slack. Each point keeps a fixed scale. Slack and strength differ by hours and knots along the Sound, so pick the point nearest your water; a click on the map gives the local current.

Method
: NOAA: CO-OPS tidal current predictions at harmonic stations LIS1001 (The Race), LIS1021 (Branford Reef), LIS1036 (Execution Rocks) and LIS1038 (Throgs Neck Bridge), at the bin nearest the surface (6 to 14 ft), every 30 minutes, with NOAA's slack and maximum times. NECOFS: the FVCOM surface current at the model element nearest each station (within 1 km), projected onto NOAA's flood direction there, every 2 hours {ref}`[1] <ref-chen2006fvcom>`. Flood runs west through the Race and the central Sound and east at Throgs Neck, so each point has its own axis.

Caveats
: Both are predictions: NOAA's from the tides alone, without wind or river flow; NECOFS's from a model run with them. Against NOAA over October 3 to 20, 2026, NECOFS kept time within about 10 minutes at the Race, the central Sound and Throgs Neck (correlation 0.93 to 0.98) and ran about 40 minutes early at Execution Rocks, where the current is weak and irregular (0.80). It reached about 65 percent of NOAA's strength at the Race and Throgs Neck (the jets are narrower than the model's mesh resolves) and ran about a third stronger in the central Sound.

References: [1] {ref}`Chen, Beardsley and Cowles (2006), the FVCOM system <ref-chen2006fvcom>`.

## Satellite fields

(method-map-sst)=
### Sea surface temperature

Shows
: Sea surface temperature at 0.01° (about 1 km), for the day shown.

Method
: The MUR multi-sensor analysis, which fills gaps between satellite passes {ref}`[1] <ref-chin2017mur>` {ref}`[2] <ref-jpl2015mur>`. Every layer covers one box (40.45 to 41.45°N, 73.9 to 71.8°W) and is cut to the currents model's water, so all layers share one coastline.

Caveats
: The skin of the water; buoy sensors sit about 1 m down. Three color ranges, switched in the key under the map. Day (the default) spans the lowest to the highest temperature on the day shown, the most detail across the water. 90 days spans the days the time bar covers, one scale as the time moves, so the season's change shows. In both, colors mean different temperatures from one range to the next. Year is one fixed scale all year: even steps from 1.5 to 25.5 °C (about the 0.5th to 99.5th percentile of 2022 to 2026 over this box), compressed beyond out to -2 and 28 °C. Both use cmocean thermal hues {ref}`[3] <ref-thyng2016cmocean>`; on the dark theme the coldest colors are lifted so cold water stays visible. A typical day spans only about 2 °C across the box, so lines every 1 °C mark the fronts that color alone would hide, with fainter half-degree lines from April to November, when the spread is narrowest.

References: [1] {ref}`Chin, Vazquez-Cuervo and Armstrong (2017), the MUR analysis <ref-chin2017mur>`; [2] {ref}`NASA/JPL (2015), MUR SST v4.1 <ref-jpl2015mur>`; [3] {ref}`Thyng et al. (2016), cmocean: colormaps for oceanography <ref-thyng2016cmocean>`.

(method-map-chl)=
### Chlorophyll-a

Shows
: Surface chlorophyll-a in mg/m³ on a log scale, about 750 m pixels.

Method
: For each pixel, the most recent clear view across the VIIRS sensors (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) within 7 days; older pixels are fainter. A one-pixel band along the coast is dropped. Background: {ref}`[1] <ref-hu2012chlorophyll>`.

Caveats
: Biased high in turbid water and near the shore.

References: [1] {ref}`Hu, Lee and Franz (2012), chlorophyll-a algorithms <ref-hu2012chlorophyll>`.

(method-map-kd490)=
### Water clarity (Kd490)

Shows
: The diffuse attenuation coefficient at 490 nm, in m⁻¹; higher is murkier.

Method
: As for chlorophyll-a. Background: {ref}`[1] <ref-wang2009kd490>`.

Caveats
: An optical proxy, not a turbidity reading in NTU.

References: [1] {ref}`Wang, Son and Harding (2009), Kd(490) in turbid waters <ref-wang2009kd490>`.
